<x_0.1445><y_0.0>But any degree of temper that is given to feel makes
a very important change in this respect. In the first
place, it acquires magnetifm more flowly by induction
than an equal and similar piece of common iron, and fi-
nally acquires lefs. Thefe differences are easily exa-
minded by the deviations which it causes in the manner's
needle from the magnetic meridian, and by its attrac-
tion.<x_0.9902><y_0.107><class_Text>

<x_0.1455><y_0.1078>When the inducing magnet is removed, fome mag-
netifm remains in the fleet bar, which retains the pola-
rity which it had in the neighbourhood of the magnet.<x_0.9873><y_0.1508><class_Text>

<x_0.1465><y_0.15>Steel tempered to the degree fit for watch springs
acquires a strong magnetism, which it exhibits imme-
diately on the removal of the magnet. But it diffipates
very fat; and, in a very few minutes, it is reduced to
lefs than one half of its intensity while in contact with
the magnet, and not two thirds of what it was imme-
diately on removal from it. It continues to diffipate for
fome days, though the bar be kept with care; but the
difipation diminishes fatt, and it retains at least one-
third of its greatest power for any length of time, unlefs
carelelsly kept or injudiciously treated.<x_0.9863><y_0.3063><class_Text>

<x_0.1475><y_0.3055>Steel tempered for frong cutting tools, fuch as chifels,
punches, and drills for metal, acquires magnetifm fill
more flowly by induction, and acquires lefs of it while
in contact with the magnet; but it retains it more firm-
ly, and finally retains a greater proportion of what it
had acquired.<x_0.9795><y_0.3906><class_Text>

<x_0.1436><y_0.3898>Steel made as hard as poffible, is much longer in ac-
quiring all the magnetifm which limple juxtapofition
can give to it. It acquires lefs than the former; but it
retains it with great firmnefs, and finally retains a much
greater proportion.<x_0.9785><y_0.4617><class_Text>

<x_0.1426><y_0.4609>Such ores of iron as are futiceptible of magnetifm,
are nearly like hard fleet in their respects; that is, in
the time necessary for their _greatell_ impregnation, and
in the durability of the acquired magnetifm. They
differ exceedingly in respect to the degree of power
which they can attain by mere juxtapolition, and the
varieties feem to depend on heterogeneous mixture.
We must observe, that few ores of iron are futiceptible
of magnetifm in their natural flate. The ordinary ores,
confiling of the metal in the flate of an oxyd, and com-
bined with fulphur, are not magnetizable while remain-
ing in that flate. Moft ores require roafting, and a fort
of cementation, in contact with inflammable fubflances.
This matter is not well understood; but it would feem
that complete metallization is far from being the moft fa-
vourable condition, and that a certain degree of oxyda-
tion, and perhaps fome other composition, yet unknown,
make the best loaditones. But all this is extremely
obcure. The late Dr Gowin Knight made a compoli-
tion which acquired a very frorng and permanent mag-
netifm, but the fetret died with him. Dr Gilbert
fpeaks of familiar compositions, in which ferrugineous
clays were ingredients; but we know nothing of the flate
of the metal in them, nor their mode of acquiring mag-
netifm.<x_0.9775><y_0.8141><class_Text>

<x_0.1289><y_0.8133>It is of peculiar importance to remark that the ac-
quilition of magnetifm is gradual and progrelive, and
that the gradation is the more perceptible in proportion
as the fleet is of a harder temper. When a magnet is
brought to one end of a bar of common iron, its remote
extremity, unlefs exceedingly long, acquires its utmoft
magnettim immediately. But when the north pole of<x_0.9609><y_0.9164><class_Text>
